questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to look after a goldfish in a small bowl at home
Whether our ability to focus is really getting shorter
Why smartphones are becoming cheaper every year
How newspapers report science stories to the public
questions.why: Neil says they're talking about attention spans and asking if they are shrinking.

questions.q: What did the Microsoft report claim?
options: Attention spans rose from 8 seconds to 12 seconds since 2000
Goldfish can focus for 12 seconds, longer than most people
People look at their phones for 12 hours a day on average
Attention spans fell from 12 seconds in 2000 to 8 seconds
questions.why: Neil says the average attention span was 12 seconds in 2000 and has fallen to eight.

questions.q: What do many people blame for this change?
options: Digital media and smartphones
Watching too much television
Not getting enough sleep
Working longer hours
questions.why: Catherine says 2000 was just before the boom in digital media and smartphones, which many blame.

questions.q: What attention span are goldfish said to have?
options: Three seconds
Eight seconds
Nine seconds
Twelve seconds
questions.why: Neil says goldfish reportedly have an attention span of nine seconds, one more than humans.

questions.q: What did the BBC programme More or Less discover about the Microsoft claim?
options: It was completely correct and based on good research
The research only studied children in American schools
It couldn't find the research the report was based on
Microsoft had tested goldfish in its own laboratory
questions.why: They couldn't find evidence of the research Microsoft quoted in its report.

questions.q: What did the psychologist tell More or Less about 'attention span'?
options: It is a common term but hard to measure scientifically
It is easy to measure with a simple test on a computer
It is only important for students who are taking exams
It is the same for everyone, whatever their age
questions.why: Neil says there are problems with measuring attention spans; the term is 'not very scientific'.

questions.q: What is Dr Gemma Briggs's view?
options: Smartphones have seriously damaged our brains and memory
People can no longer focus on one single task for very long
Attention spans are exactly the same as they were before
We may switch attention more, but can still focus when needed
questions.why: She says switching ability may have developed, but that doesn't mean we can't sustain attention on another task.

options: Humans really are worse at paying attention than goldfish now
Our attention may be fine; we just choose to look at phones more
We should all stop using smartphones for a few hours a day
Multitasking is bad for us and makes us much less productive
questions.why: She says maybe attention spans aren't getting shorter, 'we just choose to look at our phones a lot more'.
